newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Poll gives Bulgaria's UDF and allies 62 pct support.
newsitem.headline: Poll gives Bulgaria's UDF and allies 62 pct support.

text.p: Bulgaria's Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) and its coalition allies would win up to 62 percent support if general elections were held now, an opinion poll showed on Friday.

"If early elections were held now the United Democratic Forces (UDF plus allies) would win maximum support between 60 and 62 percent," Jivko Georgiev of the Bulgarian branch of Gallup polling agency told a news conference.
The UDF led month-long mass protests in January which forced the ruling ex-communist Socialist Party to stand down. General elections have been called for April 19, 20 months ahead of schedule.

All Bulgarian political parties have pledged their support for a tough reform programme agreed by the interim cabinet and the International Monetary Fund to stabilise the shattered economy in the coming years.
Support for the UDF could fall to 55 percent as enthusiasm from street protests gives way to everyday economic hardship, said Georgiev.

The survey showed 16-17 percent support for the Socialists, who lost power after failing to cope with a deep economic crisis. They won parliamentary elections in December 1994 but lost support as the economy worsened.
Georgiev said the Socialists could gain a further three percentage points from voters who are reluctant to admit their affiliation to interviewers.
Some 40 parties and coalitions will take part in the elections, but Georgiev saw only four entering parliament.

Two new parties are seen jumping the four percent vote barrier required for admission to the assembly, the National Salvation Union (NSU) with six to seven percent, and the Euro-Left with 4.5 to six percent, he said.
The Euro-Left has attracted Socialists who were disappointed with the previous government.

The NSU groups the ethnic Turkish Movement for Rights and Freedoms, which split from the UDF coalition at the last moment, an agrarian party and the Liberal Democratic Alternative set up by former president Zhelyu Zhelev.
The Bulgarian Business Bloc, which presented itself at the presidential elections as an alternative to the two main parties, is seen scoring 3.6 to five percent.

Gallup-Bulgaria estimates the election turnout at 74 percent, but the lacklustre campaign has attracted little interest so far, and fewer than 25 percent of the voters follow debates broadcast on TV several times a week, said Georgiev.
Interest is expected to pick up towards the end of the campaign, he added.
